title: Mindfulness in schools
hookLine: a large UK trial found school mindfulness lessons no better than usual teaching (Kuyken et al., 2022)

cards: Third period, a classroom of teenagers. The teacher dims the lights and asks everyone to close their eyes and notice the breath. A few actually do.
One stares at the ceiling tiles. A couple in the back are trying hard not to laugh. Somebody's phone buzzes in a backpack.
On paper it's a lovely idea: teach every child, early, the skills adults pay for later. So researchers in the United Kingdom tested it properly, across a great many schools, over years.
The answer wasn't the one its supporters hoped for.

teach.b: First, the trial. A team led by Willem Kuyken ran a large study in UK secondary schools. Some schools, chosen at random, taught a mindfulness course with trained teachers.
Others kept their usual lessons on social and emotional health. Then the researchers followed the students over time. Second, the result.
The mindfulness lessons did no better than the usual teaching for students' mental health.
Not worse, not better. The researchers also reported that many students did little of the practice outside class. Third, what that does and doesn't mean.

It doesn't show that mindfulness harms young people, or that it does nothing for adults who choose it. It shows something narrower: a practice handed to a whole class, required, on a timetable, didn't do what was hoped.
One reading: choosing may matter. Fourth, an old picture of invitation.

teach.h: I STAND AT THE DOOR, AND KNOCK.
teach.b: In the book of Revelation, in the King James text, Jesus speaks to a church this way: "Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him."
Even the one knocking doesn't break the door down.
He knocks, and waits, and the door opens from the inside. Some readers hear a whole approach to practice in that picture. A practice offered can be taken up.
A practice imposed tends to get endured.

how: Some schools offer mindfulness lessons as part of their teaching; teachers of contemplative practice often stress that it works best when people choose it rather than being made to do it.

o: a big UK trial: school mindfulness lessons did no better than usual ones
a UK law that requires every student to meditate in class each day
a program that proved meditation harms teenagers' mental health

games.q: your teenager rolls their eyes at your morning practice. what do you do?
o: make them join you every morning.
mention it once, and leave the door open.
hide your practice so it never comes up.
games.why: the trial suggests a required practice doesn't do what was hoped. the picture in Revelation is a knock, and a door that opens from the inside.

practice: Bring to mind one person you've wished would try practice, or prayer, or quiet: a child, a partner, a friend, a parent.

Notice any pushing in you, the wanting them to, and breathe with it until it softens into something simpler: wishing them well, whether they ever sit or not. If you pray, you can hold them that way in prayer.

wordCard.voice: Mindfulness in schools. A large UK trial found mindfulness lessons no better than usual teaching, a reminder that a practice can be offered but not imposed. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: invite, don't force. The door opens from the inside. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Kuyken et al., MYRIAD trial, "Effectiveness and cost-effectiveness of universal school-based mindfulness training compared with normal school provision" (Evidence-Based Mental Health)
